extracted.intended_audience: IP office staff, policymakers, researchers and practitioners interested in design statistics and design protection
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize WIPO's statistical and procedural standards for industrial design applications, registrations and examinations, and the metrics used to compare offices and origins worldwide. Includes definitions (resident/non-resident), eligibility concepts, examination types, timing and outcome measures, and data caveats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design eligibility requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: An design to be eligible for protection, it typically needs to meet certain criteria such as being new, original and of an individual character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examination procedures vary widely between offices; at some offices no substantive examination is carried out prior to registration, whereas at others a substantive examination checks the design against designs on the register for novelty and/or originality. Eligibility therefore is commonly operationalized as novelty, originality and individual character, but how those concepts are applied depends on each office's procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design right term (duration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design rights typically endure for up to 15 years from the filing date, although most European jurisdictions allow up to 25 years, while China limits the term to 10 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing 'active registrations' across offices, account for differing maximum terms (10–25 years) because these affect counts of registrations in force and average registration age.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application design count metric (designs per application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistics based on the number of designs contained in design applications – known as application design counts – improve worldwide comparability by harmonizing data between those offices that allow several designs to be contained within a single application and those that allow only one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use application design counts (not only application counts) to adjust for multiple-design applications (e.g., EUIPO average of three designs per application in 2024). This helps harmonize cross-office comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resident versus non-resident / office data versus origin data
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications received by offices from resident and non-resident applicants are referred to as office data, whereas applications filed by applicants at their home office(s) (resident applications) or at foreign offices (applications abroad) are referred to as origin data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office data provide information on destination of design activity; origin data provide information on the source. Use both perspectives to understand filing patterns (destination vs source) and to avoid misinterpreting office-level activity that may be dominated by domestic applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hague System contribution to non-resident filings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hague System filing route accounted for 35% of all non-resident designs in 2024; the Hague System provided protection in 99 countries worldwide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing non-resident filing patterns, separate Hague-system international design filings from direct national filings because the Hague System is a major route and affects distribution of non-resident designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination procedure typology
rubrics_metrics.description: Examination procedures vary widely between offices: some offices make no search and no substantive examination prior to registration, while others conduct substantive examination for novelty and/or originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of these procedural differences, comparisons of approval/rejection rates, processing times and pending application counts should be interpreted with caution; offices with no substantive examination will show much higher registration rates and shorter processing times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination outcome metrics (registration, rejection, withdrawal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Key outcome metrics include share of processed applications registered, total rejections, and withdrawals or abandonments (e.g., EUIPO registered 98.5% of processed applications in 2024; rejection rates elevated at some offices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report these outcome metrics together (registered/rejected/withdrawn) and note that high withdrawal shares may indicate different procedural or applicant behaviours. Provide office-level examples to contextualize rates (e.g., high rejection rates in certain offices; high withdrawals in others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pending applications definition and counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Potentially pending applications are taken to be all design applications, at any stage in the process, awaiting a final decision by an office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When counting pending applications, use the broad definition above. Note that offices report widely varying numbers of potentially pending applications (e.g., US: 76,665; Republic of Korea: 18,991; EUIPO: 5,391), which can reflect different processing practices and reporting conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Processing-time metrics (first office action and final decision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Processing time metrics reported include days to first office action and days to final office decision for an application (office-level averages are reported).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use both metrics to assess timeliness; first action vs final decision can vary greatly across offices (examples: EUIPO average under 4 days; US 619 days; Thailand 720 days). Report both and caution that procedural differences and backlog/pending definitions affect comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active registrations and average registration age
rubrics_metrics.description: Active registrations are registrations in force; statistics report total active registrations and average registration age by office (e.g., average age in 2024: Spain 11.2 years, UK 3 years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report both the count of registrations in force and the distribution by registration year (cohort survival), because different term lengths and renewal behaviours influence the stock of active registrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design intensity metrics (per GDP and per population)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design intensity is measured by resident application design count per USD 100 billion of GDP and resident design count per million population, enabling cross-economy comparisons of design output relative to size and development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use both metrics to normalize design activity. The report suggests plotting resident design count per capita against GDP per capita to visualize intensity relative to development level; points above the fitted line indicate higher-than-expected design intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry-sector grouping using Locarno classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Group the 32 Locarno classes into 12 industry sectors to highlight important sectors for design filings (e.g., furniture and household goods; textiles and accessories; tools and machines; ICT and audiovisual; electricity and lighting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report sectoral concentration (e.g., top three sectors' share) for offices and origins to show sectoral specialization; many top offices have 40–82% of classes concentrated in three sectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration versus application counts and design counts in registrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between the number of applications registered and the number of designs contained in registrations (registration design counts), because registrations may contain multiple designs and totals affect comparability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report both registrations (application-level) and registration design counts to capture total protected designs. For example, registrations contained about 1.27 million designs in 2024, and China accounted for about 51.1% of that total.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data caveats and comparability warnings
rubrics_metrics.description: WIPO notes that every effort has been made to compile procedural data based on common definitions and concepts, but procedural differences make it extremely difficult to fully harmonize such data. Therefore, caution should be exercised when making comparisons across offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state limitations when presenting cross-office comparisons: incomplete reporting, omission of elements (leading to incomplete application-processed totals), and differing definitions of stages/outcomes can bias comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cohorts and survival (registration-age cohort analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyse registrations by year of registration to assess cohort survival (e.g., more than one-quarter of designs registered in 2006 were still in force in 2024; more than 80% of designs registered in 2020 remained valid in 2024).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cohort analysis to evaluate durability and renewal patterns of design rights across offices, and to interpret the stock of active registrations in light of term lengths and renewal behaviour.
